title: Advanced Python: OOP, Data & Flask
intro: This term you learn to organise code with classes, study data with Pandas and charts, and put Python on the web with Flask. You will finish with a school results dashboard that runs in a browser.
termProject: SchoolBoard: a Flask results dashboard for a Nigerian secondary school class, using a Student class, Pandas for averages and WAEC-style grades, and charts, all with clearly labelled made-up practice data.

weeks.title: Classes: a mould for objects
weeks.goal: Create a class with __init__ and methods, and make objects from it.
weeks.learn: A class is like a block-moulding machine: one mould, many blocks. Each block (object) has its own data, like each student having their own name and scores. __init__ runs when a new object is made and sets its data with self. Methods are actions the object can do, like working out its own average.

research.q: Ask a teacher: what information do you keep about each student's results?
research.tip: Those pieces of information become the attributes of your Student class (use made-up names in code).

weeks.title: Inheritance: Danfo is a Vehicle
weeks.goal: Use inheritance, super() and __str__ to build a child class from a parent class.
weeks.learn: A danfo and a keke are both vehicles: they have plate numbers and seats. Inheritance lets Danfo get everything from Vehicle and add its own extras, like the conductor's call. super() runs the parent's setup. An underscore name like _passengers means 'please change this only through methods', which is called encapsulation.

research.q: Ask a driver or conductor: how many passengers does your bus or keke carry, and what do you do when it's full?
research.tip: Their answer gives you the seats number and the 'full' rule for your class.

weeks.title: Modules and packages: share your tools
weeks.goal: Put a function in your own module, import it, and use a standard library module.
weeks.learn: A module is a .py file full of tools, like a toolbox a mechanic carries from car to car. You import it to use its tools in another file. Python already has many built-in modules, like statistics. Packages from other people are installed with pip, inside a virtual environment so each project keeps its own tools.

research.q: Ask a teacher or older student: what are the WAEC grade bands, from A1 to F9?
research.tip: Check the bands they give you against the code; if they differ, ask a second teacher.

build.task: Make a grades.py module with a WAEC-style grade function and use it from main.py.
steps: Create grades.py with BANDS and grade()
Create main.py in the same folder
Run main.py
Try: python -m venv venv, then activate it and pip install pandas for next week
build.code:
# ---- file: grades.py (your own module) ----
BANDS = [(75, "A1"), (70, "B2"), (65, "B3"), (60, "C4"), (55, "C5"),
         (50, "C6"), (45, "D7"), (40, "E8"), (0, "F9")]

def grade(score):
    for lowest, letter in BANDS:
        if score >= lowest:
            return letter

# ---- file: main.py ----
import grades
from statistics import mean      # built-in module

scores = [78, 64, 51, 39]        # practice scores
for s in scores:
    print(s, "->", grades.grade(s))
print("Class mean:", mean(scores))

opts: A .py file with tools you can import

weeks.title: Pandas: a spreadsheet inside Python
weeks.goal: Load practice tuck-shop sales into a Pandas DataFrame, add a column and filter rows.
weeks.learn: Pandas gives Python a table called a DataFrame, like a spreadsheet the code can read. Each column has a name, like puff_puff or zobo. You can add new columns from old ones, find the best day, and filter rows that match a rule. The data today is MADE-UP practice data for a school tuck-shop.

research.q: Ask the school tuck-shop seller or a food vendor: which snack sells fastest, and on which day?
research.tip: Compare their answer to what your practice data shows; real data beats guessing.

build.task: Build a DataFrame of a week's practice tuck-shop sales, total it and find the best day.
steps: Activate your venv and run: pip install pandas
Type the code into tuckshop.py
Run it and read each output
Save the CSV; we use it again in Week 6
build.code:
import pandas as pd

# PRACTICE DATA (made up): a school tuck-shop's weekly sales, in units sold
sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "day":       ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri"],
    "puff_puff": [40, 35, 50, 30, 60],
    "meat_pie":  [12, 15, 10, 18, 20],
    "zobo":      [25, 20, 30, 22, 35],
})

sales["total"] = sales["puff_puff"] + sales["meat_pie"] + sales["zobo"]
print(sales)

best = sales.loc[sales["total"].idxmax(), "day"]
print("Best day:", best)

print("Days when zobo sold more than 24:")
print(sales[sales["zobo"] > 24])

print(sales[["puff_puff", "meat_pie", "zobo"]].sum())
sales.to_csv("tuckshop.csv", index=False)

weeks.title: Flask: your first Python website

weeks.learn: Flask is a small Python web framework, like Laravel was for PHP. @app.route is a decorator that says 'when someone visits this address, run this function'. weeks.title: Results dashboard: Flask + Pandas
weeks.goal: Combine Flask and Pandas to show a practice results dashboard with an average and top student.
weeks.learn: Today all your Year 3 skills meet. Pandas reads a CSV of practice results and does the maths. Flask turns the answer into a web page anyone on the school network can open. to_html() turns a DataFrame into a neat table. This is the heart of your term project: a school results dashboard.

research.q: Ask a teacher or principal: what one number would you want to see first on a results dashboard?
research.tip: Put that number at the top of your dashboard; design for the real user.

build.task: Build a Flask page that reads results.csv with Pandas and shows class average, top student and a table.
steps: Create results.csv with: name,maths,english and 4 made-up students
Type the code into dashboard.py
Run it and open the page
Add a third subject column and refresh
build.code:
# results.csv (PRACTICE DATA, made up), one row per line: # name,maths,english / Tolu,78,70 / Emeka,61,66 / Aisha,45,58 from flask import Flask, render_template_string import pandas as pd app = Flask(__name__) PAGE = '''

SS2 Results Dashboard (practice data)

Class average: {{ avg }} | Top student: {{ top }}

{{ table|safe }} ''' @app.route("/") def dashboard(): df = pd.read_csv("results.csv") subjects = df.columns.drop("name") df["average"] = df[subjects].mean(axis=1).round(1) top = df.loc[df["average"].idxmax(), "name"] return render_template_string(PAGE, avg=round(df["average"].mean(), 1), top=top, table=df.to_html(index=False)) if __name__ == "__main__": app.run(debug=True)

opts: So nobody thinks made-up numbers are real
